Weather
wĕth´ẽr
n. (the state of the sky; in the Gospels, the sign men can read and the sign they will not — Greek eudia and cheimon)
Old English weder, air, sky, storm. The Greek eudia is fair weather, literally good sky; cheimon is winter or foul weather.

Biblical Definition

Weather occurs in the Authorized Version chiefly in the Lord's rebuke to men who could forecast a sky and not a Saviour. “When it is evening, ye say, It will be fair weather: for the sky is red” (Mat 16:2), “And in the morning, It will be foul weather to day: for the sky is red and lowring. O ye hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky; but can ye not discern the signs of the times?” (Mat 16:3). The Pharisees and Sadducees had come asking for a sign from heaven — while standing in front of the Man whose works they had already seen. The rebuke is not against reading the weather, which is ordinary wisdom, but against a capacity for evidence that stops exactly where repentance would begin. Job places fair weather under God's hand and joins it to something greater: “Fair weather cometh out of the north: with God is terrible majesty” (Job 37:22). And Solomon uses weather for a lesson in pastoral tact: “As he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, and as vinegar upon nitre, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart” (Pro 25:20) — cheerfulness applied to grief does not warm the mourner; it strips him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines weather as the state of the air or atmosphere with respect to heat or cold, wetness or dryness, calm or storm, clearness or cloudiness.

expand to see more

WEATH'ER, n. The state of the air or atmosphere with respect to heat or cold, wetness or dryness, calm or storm, clearness or cloudiness, or any other meteorological phenomena.

2. Change of the state of the air.

WEATH'ER, v.t. To sustain the trying effect of; to bear up against and overcome; as, to weather a storm.

LOW'RING, ppr. Appearing dark, gloomy or threatening, as the sky.

Key Scripture

Matthew 16:2 — "He answered and said unto them, When it is evening, ye say, It will be fair weather: for the sky is red."

Matthew 16:3 — "And in the morning, It will be foul weather to day: for the sky is red and lowring. O ye hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky; but can ye not discern the signs of the times?"

Job 37:22 — "Fair weather cometh out of the north: with God is terrible majesty."

Proverbs 25:20 — "As he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, and as vinegar upon nitre, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart."

Modern Corruption

Unbelief presents itself as a want of evidence, when the Lord identifies it as a refusal to read evidence already in hand.

expand to see more

The men who asked for a sign from heaven were competent observers — they read the evening sky and the morning sky and were usually right. The Lord calls them hypocrites, not fools, because the failure was not intellectual. The same faculties that weighed the red sky refused to weigh the healings, the feedings, the cleansed lepers and the raised dead. This is the standing answer to unbelief that presents itself as evidential caution. A man who applies to the claims of Christ a standard he applies nowhere else in his life is not being careful; he is protecting a conclusion he reached before the evidence arrived.

Proverbs 25:20 belongs in this entry for the sake of the heavy-hearted, and it corrects the church rather than the world. Singing songs to a heavy heart is likened to taking away a man's coat in cold weather — well meant, and it leaves him colder. Cheerfulness pressed on grief does not lift it; it isolates the mourner and teaches him to hide. Scripture's instruction is to weep with them that weep, and Job's comforters were at their best in the seven days they said nothing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek eudia (G2105), fair weather — Matthew 16:2 only; cheimon (G5494), winter, foul weather — Matthew 16:3; Hebrew zahab (H2091), golden brightness, rendered fair weather in Job 37:22.

expand to see more

Greek eudia (G2105) — fair weather, literally a good sky; Matthew 16:2, its only occurrence.

Greek cheimon (G5494) — winter, stormy weather; Matthew 16:3, Matthew 24:20, Acts 27:20.

Greek stugnazo (G4768) — to be gloomy, lowring; Matthew 16:3, and Mark 10:22 of the rich young ruler's face.

Hebrew zahab (H2091) — gold, golden brightness; Job 37:22, where fair weather comes out of the north.

Hebrew nether (H5427) — nitre; Proverbs 25:20, on which vinegar reacts violently.

Usage

"“Ye can discern the face of the sky; but can ye not discern the signs of the times?”"

"“Fair weather cometh out of the north: with God is terrible majesty”."

"“He that singeth songs to an heavy heart” — a coat taken away in the cold."
